cards.front: Which part of the chloroplast hosts the light-dependent reactions?
cards.back: The **thylakoid membranes**, which hold chlorophyll in photosystems alongside electron carriers and the enzyme that makes ATP.
cards.hint: Think about where the green pigment sits.

cards.front: Which part of the chloroplast hosts the light-independent reaction?
cards.back: The **stroma**, where dissolved enzymes fix $\text{CO}_2$ close to the ATP and reduced NADP supplied by the thylakoids.

cards.front: How does stacking thylakoids into grana help photosynthesis?
cards.back: Stacking packs a large area of thylakoid membrane into a small volume, so more pigments, electron carriers and ATP-making enzymes fit in and more light is absorbed.
cards.hint: Think about how much pigment can fit in a small space.

cards.front: Which fluid fills most of a chloroplast and surrounds the thylakoids?
cards.back: The **stroma**, a fluid holding carbon-fixing enzymes, starch grains, lipid droplets, DNA and ribosomes.
A **granum** is a stack of flattened, fluid-filled thylakoid sacs, like coins. The plural is grana.
cards.hint: Think about how the sacs are arranged.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to call a single flattened sac a granum?
cards.back: A single sac is one **thylakoid**. A granum is the whole stack of thylakoids, so one sac alone is not a granum.
cards.hint: Count how many sacs make up one unit.

cards.back: A **strip of thylakoid membrane** linking one granum to the next. The thylakoid interiors are joined, forming one connected network.
The **double membrane**, made of an outer and an inner membrane, that encloses a chloroplast and controls which substances enter and leave.

cards.front: Why can an animal cell not carry out photosynthesis?
cards.back: It has no **chloroplasts**, the organelles that contain the thylakoids and stroma where photosynthesis takes place.
cards.hint: Compare the organelles found in plant and animal cells.

cards.front: Why does a chloroplast contain its own DNA and ribosomes?
cards.back: They let the chloroplast make some of its **own proteins** in the stroma, which can be used inside it without being imported.

cards.front: What happens to ADP and NADP after the stroma reaction uses ATP and reduced NADP?
cards.back: They return to the **thylakoid membranes** to be recharged, so the light-dependent reactions can make more ATP and reduced NADP.
cards.hint: Follow the molecules from the thylakoids to the stroma and back.

cards.front: Why is the thylakoid space kept small?
cards.back: Because it is small, **protons** that accumulate there during the light-dependent reactions build up quickly and form a gradient across the membrane.
cards.hint: Think about what the light-dependent reactions push into this space.
